name: Bianca Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say is confidential, so you can give me the public version and the private one. Can you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the mountain crew, so we look after the lines that run up the pass to the ski village and the little hamlets above the tree line. In summer it's maintenance, replacing poles that the frost has pushed out of the ground. In winter it's avalanches and ice on the lines, and sometimes the snow is so deep we go up on a tracked vehicle, a snowcat, with the tools strapped on the back.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the mountain, and I love that the people up there know us by name. The hard part is the hours in winter and the money. Our district pays at the lower end, and my husband Daniel and I are still paying off the loan for his carpentry van and tools. We married last year, and between that and the loan we've got maybe two or three weeks saved.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Do you use AI tools at all?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sometimes. Daniel's sister showed me how to use one to write his invoices and quotes properly, so I do that on Sunday nights. At work, not really, maybe once to explain a new safety rule in simpler words.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and nothing more, like a good calculator. At work we'd say the same and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be fine with that. It still helps with Daniel's invoices, and my job stays the same. I'd rather things change slowly anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going as normal. Pay down the van loan as fast as we can, about two hundred extra a month if winter overtime is good. Start saving properly once that's done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the van loan mean for your plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the thing between us and starting a family. We said once the van is paid off, we'll try for a baby. Every extra storm callout this winter is a step closer to a nursery.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who decides when you start a family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both of us, and God, I suppose. But the money decides the timing more than I'd like to admit.

S0.say: It's a useful tool and nothing more, like a good calculator. Her crew would say the same and get on with it.
S0.think: She'd be fine with it, since AI still helps with her husband's invoices and her own job stays the same. She prefers slow change anyway.
S0.do: Keeps working and pays down the loan on her husband's van and tools, about two hundred extra a month when winter overtime is good. Plans to save properly once it's cleared.
S0.quote: Every extra storm callout this winter is a step closer to a nursery.
S0.fieldNote: Bianca's life plans hinge on clearing the van loan, after which she and Daniel want a baby. She's a light, practical AI user through her husband's business. Overtime is her main lever on the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say change is part of life and people should learn what they need to. Businesses have to keep up. I'd say that to my crew, and I'd tell the younger ones to get on the courses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm a bit worried. The company might use drones to check lines up the pass instead of sending us on the snowcat, which would cut overtime. Overtime is how we're paying the loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a few people had tried the new systems, then learn them properly. I'd use the AI more for Daniel's quotes, since that's working. And I'd try to save a bit more, maybe by cutting the eating out we do after Mass.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Nothing urgent, just something to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your pay is overtime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In winter, nearly a third. If a drone does the avalanche check, that's not my job gone, but it's our baby pushed back a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if overtime dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the company really, they have to stay competitive. Maybe the regulators who make every job need so much paperwork that machines look cheaper. But mostly I'd just get on with it.

S1.say: Change is part of life, businesses have to keep up, and people should learn what they need to. She'd tell the younger crew to get on the courses.
S1.think: She's a bit worried that drones checking the pass would cut the winter overtime that pays off the van loan.
S1.do: Waits until colleagues have tried new systems, then learns them properly. Uses AI more for her husband's quotes and cuts back on eating out after Mass to save a bit more.
S1.feel: Uneasy, something to watch rather than urgent.
S1.quote: If a drone does the avalanche check, that's not my job gone, but it's our baby pushed back a year.
S1.fieldNote: Her worry is not losing her job but losing the overtime that sets the timing for a baby. She defends the company and blames regulation instead, which fits her free-market views. She'd follow, not lead, on new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. This is AGI by 2028. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs to slow down, and businesses should look after their own people. Families and churches will have to carry a lot of people for a while. I'd say that at work and to my parents.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. We have two weeks of money, a loan, and Daniel's carpentry probably gets hit too if robots can build. And we wanted a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First, we'd put off the baby, which would break my heart. I'd sell my little car and get lifts in Daniel's van, and we'd maybe rent out our spare room to a seasonal worker at the ski village. I'd work every overtime shift while there still was overtime, and I'd talk to my parents about whether we could lean on them if we had to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Daniel that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we'll be all right, we've got each other and our families. I'd say it like I believed it, and then I'd go and pray in the kitchen where he couldn't hear me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said businesses should look after their people. Do you trust them to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. The family firms in the valley would. The big ones, I'm not sure. They'd do what the numbers say.

S2.say: This needs to slow down and businesses should look after their own people. Families and churches will have to carry many people for a while.
S2.think: She'd be scared, with two weeks of money, a loan, a husband whose carpentry could be hit too, and plans for a baby.
S2.do: Puts off having a baby, sells her own car to share Daniel's van, considers renting the spare room to a seasonal ski worker. Works every overtime shift while it lasts and asks her parents whether they could lean on them.
S2.feel: Alarmed and sick in her stomach.
S2.quote: I'd say it like I believed it, and then I'd go and pray in the kitchen where he couldn't hear me.
S2.fieldNote: Putting off a baby is the heaviest cost she names, and it comes first. She would reassure Daniel and then pray alone, which shows the gap between her public calm and private fear. Her trust in business holds for family firms but not big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now AGI by 2031. The same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people work at it. Learn something new, help each other out. I'd say it at church and to my crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years makes me think about helping Daniel build up his carpentry. Robots will probably come for that too eventually, but custom work for the chalets up the mountain might last longer than line work. People with money like things made by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the line job, and on weekends I'd learn the business side of his carpentry, quotes, ordering, the website. I'd use AI tools more for that, since I've seen it works. We'd save what we can, and maybe start trying for a baby in the second year if things look all right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel like we had a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think handmade work would last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the people who buy chalets up there are paying for a story. Rich people don't want a robot kitchen, they want to know Daniel planed the wood himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes between two years and five for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, we just protect ourselves. Five years, we can build something, maybe even have the baby. It's the difference between hiding and planning.

S3.say: Five years is enough to prepare if people work at it, by learning something new and helping each other. She'd say it at church and to her crew.
S3.think: She'd help her husband build up his carpentry, betting that custom work for mountain chalets would outlast line work because wealthy buyers value handmade things.
S3.do: Keeps the line job and learns the business side of Daniel's carpentry on weekends, using AI for quotes, ordering and the website. Saves what they can and might start trying for a baby in the second year.
S3.quote: Rich people don't want a robot kitchen, they want to know Daniel planed the wood himself.
S3.fieldNote: Five years shifts her from protecting to building, centred on the family business. Her bet on handmade work for wealthy chalet owners is shrewd and specific. The baby moves back into view.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one, AGI by 2036. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to raise a family and prepare. Teach young people trades, and keep communities strong. That's what I'd tell people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be thirty-seven. I think we'd go ahead with a baby, maybe two. I'd keep climbing for a good while and help grow Daniel's business. I'm not that worried, as long as we don't waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay off the van in the first year, then start a family. Keep working the lines and slowly move more into Daniel's business, maybe full time after five or six years. Put aside a fixed amount each month for when the line job ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but hopeful too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you want your children to go into line work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was still there, I'd be proud. But I'd want them to know a craft too, like their father. I want my kids to have something in their hands that a machine would have to copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that makes you doubt the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Daniel's work dries up too. Then it's just the two of us and two kids and no trade between us. I don't like thinking about that.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time to raise a family and prepare, by teaching young people trades and keeping communities strong.
S4.think: She'd be 37, would go ahead with a baby or two, keep climbing for a while and help grow Daniel's business. She isn't very worried if they use the time well.
S4.do: Pays off the van in the first year and starts a family. Keeps working the lines while moving into Daniel's business, perhaps full time after five or six years, and saves a fixed amount monthly.
S4.quote: I want my kids to have something in their hands that a machine would have to copy.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets her keep the life she'd planned, family first. Her remaining fear is that her husband's trade dries up too. She talks about the future in terms of what her children could do with their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because we'd have to put the baby off and we don't know for how long. What would help is apprenticeships in trades that still need people, paid properly, and some help for small family businesses like Daniel's to survive. Not just a cheque in the post.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith, and it's a big part of it for me. I don't think God made us to sit at home while machines do everything. Work is part of who we are.

headlineQuote: I don't think God made us to sit at home while machines do everything.
portrait: Bianca is a 27-year-old lineworker on a mountain crew that keeps power running up the pass to a ski village, sometimes travelling by snowcat in winter. She married Daniel, a carpenter, last year, and they have two or three weeks saved while paying off his van and tools, after which they plan to have a baby. She uses AI now and then for Daniel's invoices and trusts business more than regulators. She's calm about AI Plateau and uneasy about Steady Disruption, mainly because drones could cut her overtime. AGI by 2028 alarms her because it would mean putting off a baby, while the longer timelines let her plan to move into Daniel's carpentry and start a family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and Daniel would have to put off having a baby without knowing for how long.
whatWouldHelp: Properly paid apprenticeships in trades that still need people, and help for small family businesses like Daniel's to survive, rather than just a cheque.
